how-it-works.bodyText: Revolearn About Subjects How it works Pricing Reviews FAQs Join our team Message us on WhatsApp x² + 5x + 6 = 0 (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0 x = −2 or x = −3 “Is this a dagger which I see before me” Macbeth, Act 2: imagery of guilt → Home / How it works How our tutoring works Lessons are one-to-one, online, and planned around the individual student. This page explains how tutoring is arranged and what to expect at each stage. Message us on WhatsApp Explore subjects Arranging tutoring From first enquiry to ongoing lessons, the process is straightforward and there is no obligation at any stage. 01 Get in touch Tell us the subject, the year group and what your child is finding difficult. We will respond with clear next steps. 02 Tutor matching We match your child with a tutor who specialises in that subject and teaches to their exam board and specification. 03 An initial lesson The first lesson establishes where your child is now and which areas need attention, and forms the basis of a learning plan. 04 Ongoing lessons Lessons run to an agreed schedule, with the plan reviewed as your child progresses and examinations approach. What lessons involve Every session is taught individually, using a shared online workspace so tutor and student can work through problems together. One-to-one throughout Lessons are never taught in groups. The tutor works with your child for the full session and adapts the pace to them. Taught to the specification Tutors teach to the exam board and tier your child's school has entered them for, using that board's past papers and mark schemes. A plan that adapts The learning plan agreed after the first lesson is reviewed as your child progresses and as examinations approach. Keeping parents informed You will know what your child is working on and how they are progressing, without having to chase for an update. A short written summary after lessons, covering what was taught and what to focus on next. A learning plan agreed after the initial lesson and reviewed as your child progresses. Direct contact with us whenever you would like a fuller picture of how things are going. Questions parents ask If your question is not answered here, please get in touch and we will respond directly. How do I get started? Send us a message on WhatsApp with the subject, your child's year group and what they are finding difficult. We will talk it through, explain how lessons work and arrange a first lesson. There is no obligation. Other ways to reach us How much do lessons cost? GCSE lessons start from £25 per hour and A-Level lessons from £30 per hour, charged per subject. The exact rate is agreed before any lessons are booked, and there is no charge for the initial conversation. See pricing How are students matched with tutors? We match on subject specialism, exam board and the specific areas a student needs help with, based on what you tell us at enquiry. If the match is not right, we will arrange an alternative tutor. What happens after the first session? The first session shows where the student is now. The tutor then sets out a learning plan with clear priorities and goals, and adapts it as lessons go on. How tutoring is arranged Is every lesson one-to-one? Yes. Every lesson is tailored to the student's goals, current understanding and next steps. Are lessons online? Yes. Every lesson is one-to-one over video call, with a shared workspace so the tutor and student can work through problems together. There are no in-person lessons. How long is each lesson? Lessons are typically one hour. Shorter or longer sessions can be arranged where that suits the student better, particularly for younger students or intensive revision. Can lessons be tailored to a student's specific needs? Yes. Lessons are planned around the individual student, whether that means addressing particular topics, preparing for mock examinations, or rebuilding confidence in areas that have become difficult. Can lessons be booked around my child's schedule? Yes. Lessons are arranged at times that work around school, extracurricular commitments and family life, including evenings and weekends subject to tutor availability. Can lessons be cancelled or rescheduled? Yes, with reasonable notice. We will confirm the notice period when you arrange lessons so that the arrangement is clear from the outset. More questions? gcse-maths-tuition.bodyText: Revolearn About Subjects How it works Pricing Reviews FAQs Join our team Message us on WhatsApp x² + 5x + 6 = 0 (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0 x = −2 or x = −3 y = x² − 4x + 3 Home / GCSE Maths GCSE Maths Tutoring GCSE Maths is assessed across three equally weighted papers, one without a calculator and two with, at either Foundation or Higher tier. Our tutoring is built around the specific topics a student finds difficult, rather than working through the specification from start to finish. LEVEL GCSE EXAM BOARDS AQA, Edexcel, OCR FORMAT One-to-one, online Message us on WhatsApp How it works What’s important for GCSE Maths The aspects of this qualification that most often determine how well a student performs. Choosing the right tier Foundation tier awards grades 1 to 5; Higher tier awards grades 4 to 9 from a more demanding starting point. The decision is usually made with the school, and it shapes how a student should prepare. Fluency with method Marks are awarded for working, not only for final answers. Students who set out their method clearly protect marks even when they make an arithmetic slip. Working without a calculator One of the three papers is sat without a calculator: Paper 1 at AQA and Edexcel, the middle paper at OCR. Confidence with fractions, percentages and standard form under timed conditions makes a measurable difference here. Applying skills in unfamiliar contexts Many questions present familiar mathematics in a worded or multi-step form. Recognising the underlying topic is a skill in itself, and it can be taught. What we cover Lessons concentrate on the areas an individual student needs, rather than working through the specification from beginning to end. The full specification Every topic on your child's exam board specification, across all six content areas (Number; Algebra; Ratio, proportion and rates of change; Geometry and measures; Probability; and Statistics), at Foundation or Higher tier. Exam technique Setting out working clearly, confidence without a calculator, and approaching multi-step and worded questions. Past papers and revision Practice with your exam board's past papers and mark schemes, and a revision plan ahead of mocks and final exams. Where marks are lost The mistakes that come up again and again in this subject, and what we do about each one. Working not written down Method marks are awarded for the steps, so a correct answer with no working still loses most of the question when one figure is wrong. Students are taught to write a fixed sequence for every multi-mark question: name the rule, substitute the values, then solve, one line each. Rounding and units applied too early Rounding at an intermediate step pushes the final answer outside the accepted range, and an answer in the wrong unit earns nothing. The technique is to carry full accuracy through the calculation, round once at the end, and underline the unit the question asked for before moving on. Non-calculator fluency left to chance One paper is sat without a calculator. Fractions, percentages, standard form and surds have to be secure by hand, so lessons include short, timed arithmetic drills alongside the main topic rather than leaving that fluency to revision. Worded questions not translated into maths Higher tier questions hide familiar methods inside unfamiliar contexts. Students are taught to annotate the question first: underline the quantities, write what is being asked in symbols, then name the topic before starting, which turns an unfamiliar problem into a standard one. How lessons progress The same three stages whenever a student starts, whether that is the first week of term or a month before the exams. How long each stage takes depends on the student. 1 Diagnosis The first lessons establish what a student can actually do, using their most recent assessment and a short diagnostic set covering number, algebra and proportion. This produces a written learning plan with the gaps listed in the order they need to be closed. 2 Closing gaps and building method Topics are taught in a sequence that respects what depends on what, so algebraic manipulation comes before trigonometry and proportion before compound measures. Each topic ends with exam-style questions marked against the mark scheme, so written method becomes routine. 3 Exam preparation Whole papers under timed conditions, then reviewed question by question: marks gained, marks available and the specific reason for each loss. Pacing is practised explicitly, including when to leave a question and return to it. How to revise GCSE Maths Practical guidance a student can use on their own, whether or not they have lessons with us. GUIDE 01 Revising for the non-calculator paper Most students revise topics and neglect arithmetic, then meet a paper where every calculation is done by hand. Build that fluency separately: ten minutes a day of fractions, percentages, standard form and surds, written out rather than done mentally. Work from the operations that appear most often: multiplying and dividing fractions, converting between fractions, decimals and percentages, simplifying surds, and estimating with powers of ten. Time yourself, mark honestly, and keep a short record of what you get wrong so the next session starts there. GUIDE 02 Choosing between Foundation and Higher Foundation awards grades 1 to 5 and Higher awards 4 to 9, so the entry sets both the highest grade available and the risk of missing a pass. Schools decide, usually from mock performance, but you can be part of that conversation. The useful question is not which tier is harder, but where a student scores more marks. A student securing 60% of a Foundation paper is in a stronger position than one scraping 25% of a Higher paper, and the Foundation route often produces a calmer, better-prepared candidate. Where a student is comfortably above a grade 5 on Foundation material, Higher is the right place to be. GUIDE 03 Using past papers properly A past paper only teaches you something if it is marked afterwards. Sit it in one go, to time, without notes. Then mark it yourself with the mark scheme open, writing beside each lost mark the reason: not known, known but method not shown, arithmetic slip, or question misread. Those four reasons lead to different action. Not known means reteaching. Method not shown means a writing habit. Slips mean non-calculator drills. Misreading means annotating the question before starting. Working through papers without sorting the losses this way is practice without feedback. How Revolearn supports GCSE Maths students An initial assessment to identify which topics are actually holding a student back. Lessons taught to the specification and tier the student's school has entered them for. Practice with past papers and mark schemes from the relevant exam board. Structured revision planning in the run-up to mocks and final examinations. What families say about Maths lessons 5.0 ★★★★★ 45 Google reviews Without a doubt the best tutor I’ve ever had. I was struggling with maths throughout my GCSEs but managed to go from a Grade 6 to a Grade 9 with the help of the tutors at Revolearn. Would highly recommend Kerem M. GCSE STUDENT All reviews teachers are wonderful and helped my brother improve in english and maths significantly! he feels comfortable answering questions and has a positive attitude towards learning. Maham N. FAMILY All reviews GCSE Maths questions parents ask Which tier should my child be entered for? Foundation awards grades 1 to 5 and Higher awards grades 4 to 9, so the entry sets both the ceiling and the risk. Schools normally decide, using mock results. Where a student is close to the boundary we will give you our honest view, including when a secure grade 5 at Foundation serves them better than a difficult 4 at Higher. How do you decide what to teach first? From the diagnostic work in the first lessons, not from the order of the textbook. Gaps that block later topics are closed first, because a student who is unsure with negatives or fractions will keep losing marks in topics that appear unrelated. How much work is expected between lessons? A short, specific set of practice after each lesson, usually 30 to 45 minutes, aimed at the topic just taught. It is reviewed at the start of the next lesson, so it forms part of the teaching rather than being optional. Do you teach to our exam board? Yes. We teach to AQA, Edexcel and OCR, and we use that board's past papers and mark schemes. Tell us the board at enquiry; if you are unsure, it is printed on the front of any school exam paper.
